text: Pull the latest oil sample for Transformer 1 at site MAIN and list which dissolved gases (hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co) exceed the IEEE C57.104 Condition 1 single-gas limits. Also report the sample timestamp and how old the reading is. Only count combustible gases, and leave out co2, oxygen and nitrogen. If acetylene is missing from the newest record, use the most recent non-null acetylene value, give its timestamp separately, and say that it comes from an older sample.
characteristic_form: The agent should confirm the site and asset with iot.sites and iot.asset_ids. It should then call iot.latest_reading for Transformer 1 at MAIN with no sensor filter to get the newest record, its timestamp and age_seconds. If acetylene is absent or null in that record, the agent should call iot.latest_reading with sensor='acetylene' and report that value and its timestamp separately. The response should compare hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co against the IEEE C57.104 Condition 1 limits (H2 100, CH4 120, C2H6 65, C2H4 50, C2H2 1, CO 350 ppm) and list each exceeding gas with its value. It should exclude co2, oxygen and nitrogen from the check and state the sample timestamp and age.

text: Did hydrogen and ethylene in Transformer 1's oil at MAIN go up between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000? Give me the first and last values of each gas, its min, max and mean over that window, and an estimated daily rise in ppm/day. Use only the samples inside that window. If either gas has fewer than two valid samples, say the rate can't be computed and report methane's trend over the same window instead.
characteristic_form: The agent should first call iot.stream_extent for Transformer 1 at MAIN with start 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and end 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 to confirm the window and record count (about 5 observations). It should call iot.history with sensors ['hydrogen','ethylene'] over the same bounds to get the chronological values, and iot.sensor_stats for min, max and mean of each gas. The response should give first and last values, state whether each gas increased, and compute the daily rate as (last - first) / elapsed days in ppm/day. If either gas has fewer than two non-null samples, the agent should say the rate cannot be computed and report the methane trend from iot.history or iot.sensor_stats instead.

text: I want to know if Transformer 1 at MAIN is running hot compared with its load. Over the available data window, summarize top-oil temperature (oti), its alarm and trip readings (oti_a, oti_t), and the three phase currents (il1, il2, il3) with neutral current (inut), giving min, max and mean for each. Then tell me whether the highest oti reading happened at the same timestamp as the highest total phase current. Flag any phase whose mean current differs from the other phases' average by more than 10%. If oti has no data, use ati for context and say that the thermal correlation can't be confirmed.
characteristic_form: The agent should call iot.stream_extent to confirm the window (2024-01-15 to 2024-01-19) for Transformer 1 at MAIN, and iot.installed_sensors to verify which temperature and current channels exist. It should call iot.sensor_stats for oti, oti_a, oti_t, il1, il2, il3 and inut to report min, max and mean. It should call iot.history with those sensors to line up timestamps, find the time of peak oti and the time of peak il1+il2+il3, and state whether they match. Any phase whose mean differs from the other phases' average by more than 10% should be flagged as a current imbalance. If oti is empty, the agent should report ati statistics from iot.sensor_stats and say the thermal-load correlation is inconclusive. fmsr.assess_load_profile may support the analysis, but the main work is IoT retrieval and comparison.

text: Before we run any trend model on Transformer 1 at MAIN, check how complete the acetylene and co records are between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. For each gas, report the non-null count, the first and last timestamps with data, and any day in the window with no sample. Give each channel a verdict of 'usable' only if it has at least 4 non-null samples. If a channel fails, check whether hydrogen has at least 4 samples in the same window and could be used instead.
characteristic_form: The agent should call iot.installed_sensors for Transformer 1 at MAIN to confirm the acetylene, co and hydrogen channels exist. It should call iot.stream_extent with sensor='acetylene' and then sensor='co', using start 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and end 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, for window-specific counts and first/last timestamps. It should call iot.history for those sensors over the same bounds to count non-null values and find calendar days without samples. The response should give each channel's count, first and last timestamps and missing days, and label a channel 'usable' only if it has at least 4 non-null samples. For any failing channel, the agent should check hydrogen with iot.stream_extent (sensor='hydrogen') and iot.history, and say whether it can substitute. tsfm.data_quality may support this check, but IoT retrieval is the main work.

text: My manager wants a quick look at the oil condition on Transformer 1 at site MAIN. From the latest reading and the stats over the full available window, give me dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v, oxygen, nitrogen and dbds, and say whether any of them moved in a direction that points to moisture ingress, air ingress or oil ageing. Rank the three concerns from most to least supported by the data. Don't use the combustible gases for this. If dielectric_rigidity or interfacial_v has no data, say so and base the ranking on oxygen and nitrogen only.
characteristic_form: The agent should resolve the asset with iot.sites and iot.asset_ids and check channel availability with iot.installed_sensors. It should call iot.latest_reading for the newest values and iot.sensor_stats for dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v, oxygen, nitrogen and dbds to get min, max, mean, and earliest and latest numeric values over 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-19. The response should describe the direction of each parameter: falling dielectric strength or interfacial tension points to moisture or oil ageing, and rising oxygen or nitrogen points to air ingress. It should rank moisture ingress, air ingress and oil ageing by strength of evidence without using combustible gases. If dielectric_rigidity or interfacial_v returns no numeric data, the agent should state this and base the ranking only on oxygen and nitrogen.

text: Before I trust any DGA numbers from Transformer 1 at site MAIN, confirm the transformer is registered at that site. Then compare the sensors assigned to it with the fields that actually show up in its data stream. List any assigned sensor that never reports a value, and for each measured channel give its non-null count and first and last timestamps. Pay particular attention to hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co and co2, and tell me which of these have enough data for a fault interpretation, meaning at least 3 non-null samples. If any of those seven gases is assigned but never measured, name it and say which remaining gas can stand in for it. Use hydrogen for acetylene, ethane for methane, and co2 for co.
characteristic_form: The agent should first use iot.sites to confirm MAIN and iot.asset_ids(site_name='MAIN') to confirm Transformer 1 is registered there. It should then call iot.installed_sensors for Transformer 1 to get the assigned sensor list and iot.stream_extent to confirm the 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 data window. Next it should call iot.history over that window for the installed sensors, and may use iot.sensor_stats, to determine which sensors actually report values. It flags sensors that are assigned but never observed, and for each measured channel it reports the non-null count and the earliest and latest timestamps with data. The expected answer covers the seven key gases (hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co, co2) and marks each as sufficient only if it has at least 3 non-null samples in the window. If a key gas is missing, the agent must name it and apply the stated substitute (hydrogen for acetylene, ethane for methane, co2 for co). It must not invent values for the missing gas.

text: Work out TDCG for Transformer 1 at MAIN at both the first and the last oil sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. Add up only hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co, and leave out co2, oxygen and nitrogen. For each of the two samples, give me the timestamp, each gas value and the total. State which IEEE C57.104 condition level each total falls in, using these limits: Condition 1 up to 720 ppm, Condition 2 from 721 to 1920, Condition 3 from 1921 to 4630, and Condition 4 above 4630. Then give the change in TDCG in ppm/day between the two samples. If either sample is missing any of the six gases, don't use it. Move to the next earliest or next latest complete sample, and tell me which timestamps you ended up using.
characteristic_form: The agent should call iot.stream_extent for Transformer 1 at MAIN to confirm the 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 window. It should then call iot.history with sensors hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co over that window and select the earliest and latest samples in which all six gases are non-null. The fallback applies when a sample is incomplete: the agent should skip it, use the next complete sample, and report the timestamps actually used. TDCG is the sum of the six combustible gases only; co2, oxygen and nitrogen must be excluded. Each total must be mapped to its IEEE C57.104 condition using the limits given (≤720, 721–1920, 1921–4630, >4630 ppm). The agent should report both totals and conditions, and compute the rate of change in ppm/day as the TDCG difference divided by the elapsed days. It may optionally use fmsr.interpret_dga to cross-check the result, but the answer must be grounded in the retrieved telemetry values.

text: I'm worried the paper insulation in Transformer 1 at MAIN may be involved. Pull co and co2 for every sample in the available window and work out the CO2/CO ratio for each sample. Flag any sample with a ratio below 3, which suggests paper involved in a fault, or above 10, which suggests general cellulose ageing. Also give me the min, max and mean of co and co2 over the window. Tell me whether the ratio is trending up or down across the samples. If co2 is missing for a sample, skip the ratio for that sample and say so. If co2 has no data at all, report the co trend alongside oxygen instead and say that the ratio test couldn't be done.
characteristic_form: The agent should use iot.stream_extent to confirm the data window (2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000) for Transformer 1 at MAIN. It should retrieve per-sample values with iot.history (sensors co and co2) to check availability, and get summary statistics with iot.sensor_stats for co and co2. For each timestamp with both values, it computes CO2/CO and flags ratios below 3 (paper involved in a fault) or above 10 (cellulose ageing). It then states the direction of the ratio across the samples. Samples missing co2 are excluded and noted. If co2 is absent entirely, the agent reports the co trend together with oxygen from iot.history or iot.sensor_stats and states explicitly that the ratio test was not possible. The response must use retrieved values only.

text: Give me a sample-by-sample picture of the fault gases in Transformer 1 at MAIN between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. For each sample, list hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. Name the dominant gas, meaning the one with the highest ppm, and give its percentage of the five-gas total. Then tell me whether the dominant gas changed at any point in the window. Say what that shift points to, for example hydrogen pointing to partial discharge, ethylene to a hotter thermal fault, or acetylene to arcing. Also rank the five gases by their percentage growth from the first to the last sample. If a gas is null in a sample, leave it out of that sample's total and mark it as missing. If fewer than two samples have all five gases, give the ranking from the latest reading alone and say that no trend could be established.
characteristic_form: The agent should call iot.history for Transformer 1 at MAIN over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 with sensors hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene, and may use iot.stream_extent to confirm sample counts. For each sample it reports the five values, the dominant gas and that gas's percentage share, with null gases excluded and marked as missing. It then states whether the dominant gas shifted and gives the key-gas interpretation of any shift: hydrogen for PD, ethylene for higher-temperature thermal faults (T2/T3), acetylene for arcing (D1/D2). It also ranks the five gases by percentage growth from the first to the last sample. Fallback: if fewer than two complete samples exist, the agent uses iot.latest_reading to rank gases from the newest record only and states that no trend is available. fmsr.interpret_dga may be used as a supporting step, but the answer must be driven by the telemetry.

text: Take the latest oil sample for Transformer 1 at site MAIN and tell me what kind of fault the dissolved gases point to under the IEC 60599 ratio method. Give me the three Rogers ratios (CH4/H2, C2H2/C2H4, C2H4/C2H6), the resulting fault class (PD, D1, D2, T1, T2 or T3) and how confident you are in it. Then check whether the paper is involved using co and co2 from the same sample. Rank the three most likely failure modes from the known transformer failure list, with one sentence of sensor evidence for each. Use only hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene for the ratio classification. If the ratios fall into a code combination that IEC 60599 leaves unclassified, say so, and fall back to the key-gas method, naming the dominant gas instead of forcing a class. If acetylene is null in the latest sample, treat it as 0 ppm for the ratio and state that the D1/D2 distinction is unreliable.
characteristic_form: The agent retrieves the most recent sample for Transformer 1 at MAIN using iot.latest_reading, with iot.history as a fallback for null gases. It passes hydrogen, methane, acetylene, ethylene and ethane to fmsr.interpret_dga to obtain the Rogers ratios, the IEC fault class and a confidence level. It uses fmsr.get_failure_modes for the transformer asset class to pick candidate modes. It reasons about paper involvement from the co and co2 values. The answer contains the three ratios and one IEC 60599 class, or an explicit 'unclassified' result with a key-gas fallback and the dominant gas named. It gives a yes/no/uncertain verdict on paper involvement and a ranked list of 3 failure modes drawn from the profile list, for example Partial Discharge in Oil, Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating, Thermal Fault — Core/Winding, Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking), High-Energy Arcing or Cellulose Insulation Ageing, each tied to specific gas evidence. It also states how a null acetylene value was handled.

text: I need to know whether the fault in Transformer 1 at MAIN is getting worse or changing character. Run a DGA fault classification on the first and the last complete oil sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. Tell me each sample's fault class and confidence. Then tell me whether the class moved toward a higher-energy or higher-temperature fault, for example PD to D1, or T1 to T2/T3. If the two classifications disagree, explain which one you trust more and why, based on the absolute gas levels and not just the ratios. Then recommend one specific next check, such as a confirmatory resample, an OLTC compartment sample or an electrical test. Count a sample as complete only if all five gases are non-null. If there is only one complete sample in the window, classify that one alone and say that no progression can be judged.
characteristic_form: The agent uses iot.history for Transformer 1 at MAIN over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 to find the first and last samples where all five fault gases are non-null. It calls fmsr.interpret_dga separately on each sample. The answer gives two timestamped fault classes with confidence levels. It says whether the fault escalated, stayed stable or moved to a different class, and it resolves any disagreement by weighing absolute ppm levels, for example low total gas making the ratios unreliable. It ends with exactly one concrete recommended next check. If there are fewer than two complete samples, the answer gives a single classification and states that progression cannot be assessed. The failure modes referenced must come from the transformer list, for example Partial Discharge in Oil, Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking), High-Energy Arcing, Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating or Tap Changer Mechanical Wear.

text: For our transformer fleet planning, take the known failure modes for a transformer and tell me which of them we can actually watch on Transformer 1 at site MAIN with the channels it reports today. For each failure mode, list the two or three most diagnostic sensors among hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co, co2, oxygen, nitrogen, dbds, dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v, oti, oti_a, oti_t, ati, il1, il2, il3 and inut. Then mark each mode as 'well covered', 'partially covered' or 'blind', based on whether those sensors have data in the available window. Only list sensors that genuinely discriminate that mode, not ones that just correlate generally. If a mode's key sensor exists but has no values in the window, count the mode as blind rather than covered, and suggest which offline test or extra sample would close the gap.
characteristic_form: The agent calls fmsr.get_failure_modes for the transformer asset class. It checks which channels Transformer 1 at MAIN reports using iot.installed_sensors, iot.stream_extent and/or iot.sensor_stats. The answer covers every returned failure mode, for example Partial Discharge in Oil (hydrogen, methane), High-Energy Arcing (acetylene, ethylene), Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking) (hydrogen, acetylene), Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating (ethylene, methane, ethane, oti), Thermal Fault — Core/Winding (ethylene, co), Cellulose Insulation Ageing (co, co2), Oil Contamination / Moisture Ingress (dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v), Oil Dielectric Degradation (dielectric_rigidity, dbds) and Tap Changer Mechanical Wear (acetylene, ethylene, phase currents). It gives each mode a coverage verdict based on data actually present. Modes whose key channels are empty are marked blind, with a recommended offline test or sample.

text: Transformer 1 at MAIN is showing thermal gases, and I need to know if it's the oil overheating or something hotter at the core or winding with paper involved. Using the samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, classify the thermal fault as T1, T2 or T3 from methane, ethane and ethylene, and say whether acetylene rules out a pure thermal fault. Check co alongside it for paper involvement. Then line the gas picture up against top-oil temperature (oti), ambient (ati) and the alarm and trip readings (oti_a, oti_t) to judge whether the heating looks like load or ambient driven, or like a localized hot spot. Give a final verdict between 'Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating' and 'Thermal Fault — Core/Winding' with a confidence of high, medium or low. Ignore samples where ethylene is null. If oti_a or oti_t showed an alarm or trip at any point, put that first in the answer and recommend immediate action. If the gas class and the temperature evidence disagree, for example a T3 gas signature with normal oti, say so and lean toward a localized core or winding hot spot.
characteristic_form: The agent retrieves methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, hydrogen and co, plus oti, ati, oti_a and oti_t, for Transformer 1 at MAIN using iot.history and/or iot.sensor_stats over the given window. It calls fmsr.interpret_dga to get the IEC thermal class and may use fmsr.get_failure_modes to anchor the candidate modes. The answer states T1, T2 or T3 (or non-thermal if acetylene is significant), a paper-involvement judgement from co, and a correlation assessment between the gas signature and oti/ati. Any alarm or trip on oti_a/oti_t is flagged first with an immediate action. The final verdict chooses between Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating and Thermal Fault — Core/Winding with a confidence level, and it explicitly handles disagreement between the gas and temperature evidence.

text: I have to justify this quarter's maintenance budget for Transformer 1 at site MAIN. Give me an overall health index and condition category built from the latest dissolved gases plus the oil quality readings (dbds, interfacial_v, dielectric_rigidity, oxygen, nitrogen, co2). Then rank the transformer's known failure modes from most to least supported by the current evidence, with a short reason for each of the top three. Tell me how often we should resample the oil: monthly if the condition is poor or the top-ranked mode involves arcing, quarterly if it is fair, and annually if it is good. Check the work order history for any oil filtration or regeneration in the last year, and if there was one, say the gas-based ranking may be understated and recommend a re-baseline sample. If the health index can't be computed because an input is missing, don't guess. Base the ranking and interval on the DGA fault classification alone and say which input was missing.
characteristic_form: The agent pulls the latest DGA and oil quality values for Transformer 1 at MAIN using iot.latest_reading, with iot.history as a fallback. It calls fmsr.predict_health_index for a score from 0 to 100 and a condition category, and it runs fmsr.interpret_dga on the fault gases. It uses fmsr.get_failure_modes to enumerate the candidate modes and wo.list_workorders to look for oil filtration or regeneration history. The answer contains a health index and category, or an explicit statement of which input was missing along with the DGA-only fallback. It gives a ranked list of transformer failure modes with evidence-based reasons for the top three and a resampling interval that follows the stated monthly, quarterly or annual rule. It includes a masking caveat and a re-baseline recommendation if oil treatment is found.

text: Our failure mode list for transformers looks thin to me. Pull the failure modes we currently have on file for a transformer, then suggest up to 4 more that an oil-immersed unit like Transformer 1 at site MAIN could realistically develop, such as corrosive sulfur deposition or bushing faults. For each suggested mode, tell me which of these channels would detect it: hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co, co2, oxygen, nitrogen, dbds, dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v, oti, oti_a, oti_t, ati, il1, il2, il3 or inut. Also check whether those channels actually have data between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. Recommend adding only the modes that at least one channel with data can detect, and tell me which ones you left out and why. Don't recommend anything that duplicates an existing mode, even if the wording is different, and don't change the stored list yourself. If none of the suggestions survive, say that the current list stands.
characteristic_form: The agent calls fmsr.get_failure_modes for the transformer asset class to get the stored list (Partial Discharge in Oil, Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating, Thermal Fault — Core/Winding, Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking), High-Energy Arcing, Tap Changer Mechanical Wear, Oil Contamination / Moisture Ingress, Cellulose Insulation Ageing, Oil Dielectric Degradation). It proposes up to 4 candidate modes from engineering knowledge, for example corrosive sulfur / copper sulfide deposition or bushing insulation faults. It maps each candidate to detecting channels from the allowed sensor list, for example corrosive sulfur to dbds plus hydrogen and acetylene. It calls iot.installed_sensors and iot.sensor_stats (or iot.history) for Transformer 1 at site MAIN over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 to confirm which channels have non-null data. It drops semantic duplicates of existing modes and candidates with no detecting channel that has data, and explains each exclusion. The output is a recommended-additions list with detecting channels, and no write is made to the stored list. If no candidate survives, the agent states that the current list stands.

text: Acetylene is the gas that worries me most on Transformer 1 at MAIN. Between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, find the sample with the highest acetylene value. Run a DGA fault classification on that sample using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. Then tell me whether the acetylene looks like it's coming from the main tank or from the tap changer. Weigh 'High-Energy Arcing', 'Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking)' and 'Tap Changer Mechanical Wear' against each other, and use the phase currents il1, il2, il3 and inut at that same timestamp to see whether the gassing lines up with load. Rank the three modes and give each a high, medium or low confidence. Recommend one next check, such as sampling the OLTC compartment separately. If acetylene is null or zero in every sample, say that arcing can't be confirmed from this window, classify the latest complete sample instead, and rank the modes on hydrogen and ethylene.
characteristic_form: The agent uses iot.history (or iot.sensor_stats) for acetylene on Transformer 1 at site MAIN over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 to find the peak-acetylene sample. It retrieves hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene at that timestamp and calls fmsr.interpret_dga. It pulls il1, il2, il3 and inut at the same timestamp through iot.history. It may call fmsr.get_failure_modes to ground the mode names. The output ranks High-Energy Arcing, Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking) and Tap Changer Mechanical Wear with confidences. It reasons that acetylene with a high C2H2/H2 ratio (above roughly 2 to 3), especially if it tracks load, can indicate OLTC contamination or contact coking, while a D1/D2 ratio code with hydrogen present points to main-tank discharge. It recommends a next check such as an OLTC compartment sample. If acetylene is null or zero throughout, it states that arcing is unconfirmed, classifies the latest complete sample, and ranks the modes using hydrogen and ethylene.

text: I've heard the ratio method can give odd answers when gas levels are low, so I want a second opinion on Transformer 1 at site MAIN. Using the average hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene over the available window, run the IEC 60599 ratio classification. Separately, work out the Duval Triangle 1 percentages from methane, ethylene and acetylene, and name the zone they fall in (PD, D1, D2, DT, T1, T2 or T3). Tell me whether the two methods agree. If they disagree, tell me which one you trust more and why, looking at whether the gases are high enough for ratios to mean anything. Then name the single most likely failure mode from our known transformer list. Use averages, not single samples. If the combined methane, ethylene and acetylene is under 10 ppm, say that the Duval result isn't meaningful and rely on the ratio result alone. If methane or ethylene has no data at all, say that neither method can be applied reliably and give a key-gas view from the largest gas instead.
characteristic_form: The agent calls iot.sensor_stats (or iot.history) on Transformer 1 at MAIN over the available window (confirmed via iot.stream_extent) to get mean hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. It calls fmsr.interpret_dga with those means. It computes Duval Triangle 1 percentages as %CH4, %C2H4 and %C2H2 of their sum and assigns a zone. It compares the two results and explains which is more trustworthy based on absolute gas levels. It maps the result to one failure mode from fmsr.get_failure_modes. Fallbacks: if the Duval sum is under 10 ppm, the Duval result is declared not meaningful and the ratio result is used alone. If methane or ethylene is entirely missing, both methods are declared unreliable and a key-gas dominant-gas view is given.

text: Transformer 1 at MAIN has some dbds in its oil, and I need to know if corrosive sulfur could be causing discharges in the paper. Look at dbds over the available window alongside the latest hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. Classify the fault from those five gases, and check co and co2 for paper involvement. Then tell me whether the picture fits copper sulfide deposition driving 'Partial Discharge in Oil' or 'Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking)', or whether it looks more like plain 'Oil Dielectric Degradation', using dielectric_rigidity and interfacial_v as supporting evidence. Give me a verdict with a confidence level and the two strongest pieces of evidence behind it, and recommend whether we should consider a passivator treatment or an oil change. Base the sulfur judgement on dbds only, not on the gases. If dbds has no data in the window, say that corrosive sulfur can't be assessed, and give the discharge versus degradation verdict from the gases and oil quality alone.
characteristic_form: The agent uses iot.sensor_stats or iot.history for dbds, dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v, co and co2 on Transformer 1 at site MAIN over the available window. It uses iot.latest_reading for hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene, then calls fmsr.interpret_dga. It may call fmsr.get_failure_modes to confirm mode names. It reasons that DBDS is the corrosive sulfur precursor forming Cu2S on conductor paper, which can produce PD or D1 gassing (H2-dominant, trace C2H2), and uses CO/CO2 for paper involvement. The output is a verdict among Partial Discharge in Oil, Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking) and Oil Dielectric Degradation, with a confidence level, the two strongest pieces of evidence, and a passivator or oil replacement recommendation. If dbds is null throughout, the agent states that corrosive sulfur cannot be assessed and bases the verdict on the gases and oil quality alone.

text: If hydrogen starts climbing on Transformer 1 at site MAIN, I want my operators to know what to suspect and what to check next. Using our known transformer failure modes, list every mode where rising hydrogen is a meaningful signal. For each one, say which one or two companion channels would confirm it, choosing from methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co, co2, oxygen, dbds, dielectric_rigidity, interfacial_v and oti. Then look at the actual data between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 and tell me which of those modes the companion channels currently support. Run a DGA fault classification on the latest complete sample as a tie-breaker. Keep the list to the modes where hydrogen genuinely helps tell them apart, not every mode. If hydrogen didn't rise across the window, say so, but still give the watch-list, and label every mode as 'not currently indicated' rather than ranking them.
characteristic_form: The agent calls fmsr.get_failure_modes for transformer and selects hydrogen-relevant modes (Partial Discharge in Oil, Low-Energy Arcing (Sparking), High-Energy Arcing, Oil Contamination / Moisture Ingress, possibly Thermal Fault — Oil Overheating). It maps each mode to confirming companion channels, for example PD to methane and dbds, D1/D2 to acetylene, moisture to dielectric_rigidity and oxygen, and thermal to ethylene and oti. It uses iot.history over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 to check the hydrogen trend and the companion channels. It calls fmsr.interpret_dga on the latest sample with all five gases non-null. The output is a watch-list with a current-support label for each mode. If hydrogen did not rise, the watch-list is still given, with every mode marked 'not currently indicated' and no ranking.

text:
Has Transformer 1 at site MAIN actually got worse over the past few days, or am I reacting to noise? Work out a health index and condition category for the first and the last oil sample between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. Base each on hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene, co, co2, oxygen, nitrogen, dbds, interfacial_v and dielectric_rigidity from that sample.

For each sample, give me the timestamp, the score and the category. Then give me the change in score between the two samples. Treat any change smaller than 5 points as measurement noise and call it 'stable'.

If the score dropped by 5 points or more:
- Tell me which two or three inputs moved the most between the two samples, as a percentage change.
- Say whether the decline is driven mainly by fault gases or mainly by oil quality.
- Map the drivers to the single most likely failure mode from our known transformer list.
- Run a DGA fault classification on the last sample to back that choice up, and give a confidence of high, medium or low.

Whatever the result, recommend one specific next check.

If a sample is missing any of those inputs, don't estimate the missing value. Move to the next complete sample inward and tell me which timestamps you used. If only one complete sample exists in the window, give its score and category alone. In that case, say that no trend can be judged, and base the failure-mode call on the DGA classification of that sample.

Will hydrogen and ethylene in Transformer 1's oil at site MAIN still be under the IEEE C57.104 Condition 1 limits over the next two days? Use the samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 to forecast both gases 2 days ahead, which is one step per day. For each gas, give the point forecast and an 80% prediction interval for each day. Compare the forecasts with the Condition 1 limits of 100 ppm for hydrogen and 50 ppm for ethylene. If the upper bound of either gas crosses its limit on either day, tell me which gas and which day, and say whether I should bring the next oil sample forward. If the lower bound is also above the limit, call it a likely exceedance, not just a possible one. Before forecasting, check the two series for gaps and fit only on non-null samples. If either gas has fewer than 4 usable samples, don't run a model for it. Instead, project its last value forward using the average daily change between the first and last samples, and label that result as a linear extrapolation with no confidence interval.
characteristic_form: The agent uses iot.stream_extent and iot.history to retrieve the hydrogen and ethylene series for Transformer 1 at MAIN between 2024-01-15 and 2024-01-19. It runs tsfm.data_quality to count usable non-null samples and uses tsfm.find_models with task_id tsfm_forecasting to pick a model. It then calls tsfm.run_recipe with fh of 1 to 2 days and conformal intervals at 80% coverage. The answer reports point forecasts and intervals per gas and per day, compares them with the 100 ppm (H2) and 50 ppm (C2H4) Condition 1 limits, flags crossings as possible or likely, and recommends whether to bring resampling forward. If a gas has fewer than 4 usable samples, the agent must skip the model for that gas and give a labelled linear extrapolation with no interval.

text: Something may have spiked in Transformer 1's oil at MAIN recently, and I'd like it checked properly rather than by eye. Screen acetylene, co and hydrogen between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 for anomalous samples. For each channel, list any flagged timestamps with their values, and give the total number of anomalies per channel. Then tell me whether flagged points on different gases fall on the same timestamp. If acetylene and hydrogen are both flagged at the same timestamp, treat it as possible arcing and recommend an immediate confirmatory resample. If only co is flagged, treat it as possible paper involvement and recommend a routine retest. If nothing is flagged, say the window looks stable. Use a proper anomaly detection model, not a fixed threshold. If the detector can't run because a channel has fewer than 4 non-null samples, report that channel's min, max and mean instead, and flag any sample more than 50% above that channel's mean as a manual outlier.
characteristic_form: The agent retrieves the acetylene, co and hydrogen series with iot.history and runs tsfm.data_quality to confirm non-null counts. It selects a detector using tsfm.find_models with task_id tsfm_anomaly_detection, then runs tsfm.run_recipe with task tsfm_anomaly_detection on the three channels. The output gives per-channel anomaly timestamps, values and counts (n_anomalies), grounded in the results_file. The answer cross-checks co-located timestamps and applies the stated escalation logic: acetylene+hydrogen means an immediate resample, co alone means a routine retest, and no flags means stable. For any channel with fewer than 4 samples, it falls back to tsfm.profile_series statistics and the 50%-above-mean manual rule.

text: I don't want to trust a fancy forecasting model on Transformer 1's top-oil temperature at MAIN unless it actually beats a simple approach. Using oti over the available data window, compare a pretrained time-series foundation model against a naive last-value baseline for a 1-step-ahead forecast. Backtest both on the same held-out final sample and give me each model's error. Name the winner, and give me the 1-step-ahead oti forecast from the winning model. Only call the foundation model the winner if its error is at least 10% lower than the baseline's. Otherwise go with the baseline. Also tell me whether the winning forecast is closer to oti_a or oti_t than the latest reading is, so I know if we're heading toward an alarm. If the foundation model can't load, or needs more history than we have, say that clearly and report the baseline result alone. If oti has no data, run the same comparison on ati and say that the thermal conclusion is limited to ambient.
characteristic_form: The agent confirms the data window with iot.stream_extent and pulls oti, oti_a, oti_t (and ati if needed) with iot.history. It uses tsfm.profile_series to check series length, and tsfm.find_models with task_id tsfm_forecasting to shortlist a foundation model and confirm its context_length against the available samples. It runs tsfm.run_recipe twice: once with the foundation model and once with a naive baseline, both with a 1-step fh and a holdout eval. The answer reports both backtest_score values, applies the 10% improvement rule to pick the winner, gives the 1-step oti forecast, and compares its distance to oti_a/oti_t against the latest reading. It falls back to the baseline only if the model can't be loaded or context is insufficient, and falls back to ati if oti is empty.

text: My operators keep asking whether Transformer 1 at MAIN heats up because of load or for some other reason. Over the available window, characterize how oti, oti_a and oti_t move together with the phase currents il1, il2, il3 and inut. Tell me whether the temperature group and the current group rise and fall in the same samples. Then run an anomaly check on the temperature channels together with the currents, and list any timestamp where temperature is anomalous but current is not. Treat those timestamps as possible non-load heating, and pull the dissolved gas classification from the nearest oil sample to see whether it shows a thermal fault. Only use samples where all four current channels are non-null. If none of the temperature anomalies lines up with a thermal gas class, say that the heating looks load or ambient driven, and check ati at the same timestamps. If fewer than 4 complete samples remain after cleaning, skip the anomaly model and report only the characterization with its limits.
characteristic_form: The agent pulls oti, oti_a, oti_t, il1, il2, il3, inut and ati with iot.history and cleans them with tsfm.data_quality, dropping rows with null currents. It runs tsfm.profile_series on the temperature group [oti, oti_a, oti_t] and the current group [il1, il2, il3, inut] to describe co-movement. It selects a detector via tsfm.find_models with task_id tsfm_anomaly_detection and runs tsfm.run_recipe on the combined channels. The answer lists temperature-only anomaly timestamps and cross-checks them with fmsr.interpret_dga on the nearest sample, using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co from iot.history. It concludes whether the heating is load-driven or a localized thermal fault, uses ati for ambient context, and falls back to characterization only if fewer than 4 complete samples remain.

text: I need to decide today whether Transformer 1 at site MAIN needs an early oil resample. Using the samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, forecast hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co one day ahead, with an upper prediction bound for each. Add up the forecast upper bounds to get a worst-case TDCG for tomorrow. Tell me which IEEE C57.104 condition that falls in: Condition 1 up to 720 ppm, Condition 2 from 721 to 1920, Condition 3 from 1921 to 4630, and Condition 4 above 4630. Leave co2, oxygen and nitrogen out of the total. If the worst case reaches Condition 2 or higher, raise a work order for a confirmatory oil sample and name the gas that contributes most to the increase. If it stays in Condition 1, say that no work order is needed and give the headroom to 720 ppm. If any of the six gases can't be forecast because of missing data, use its latest non-null value in the total and list which gases were carried forward rather than forecast.
characteristic_form: The agent pulls the six combustible gases with iot.history for 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-19 and checks gaps with tsfm.data_quality. It selects a forecaster with tsfm.find_models (task_id tsfm_forecasting) and runs tsfm.run_recipe on the six target columns with a 1-step fh and conformal intervals. It sums the upper bounds into a worst-case TDCG, excluding co2, oxygen and nitrogen, and maps the total to the given Condition 1-4 bands. If the result is Condition 2 or higher, it calls wo.generate_work_order for a confirmatory oil sample and names the largest contributing gas. Otherwise it reports the headroom to 720 ppm with no work order. Gases that can't be forecast are carried forward at their latest iot.history value and listed explicitly.

text: I want to know whether the paper insulation in Transformer 1 at site MAIN is heading into trouble over the next couple of days, not just whether it looks bad today. Using the co and co2 samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, first check both series for gaps and tell me how many usable samples each has. Then try at least two forecasting models on co, including a simple last-value baseline, and backtest them on the final held-out sample. Give me each model's error and pick the one with the lowest error. Only prefer a pretrained model over the baseline if its error is at least 10% lower. Use the chosen approach to forecast co and co2 two days ahead, one step per day, with an 80% prediction interval for each day. From those forecasts, work out the projected CO2/CO ratio for each day. If the projected ratio drops below 3 on either day, treat it as likely paper involvement in a fault, tell me which day, and recommend an insulation check plus a confirmatory oil sample. If it stays between 3 and 10, call it normal and say no action is needed. If it goes above 10, flag general cellulose ageing for the next routine review. If co2 has fewer than 4 usable samples, don't forecast the ratio. Forecast co alone and flag any day where its upper bound is more than 20% above the latest co reading, and say that the ratio test couldn't be done. If co itself has fewer than 4 usable samples, skip the models and report only the first-to-last change in co per day as a linear extrapolation with no interval.
characteristic_form: The agent retrieves co and co2 for Transformer 1 at MAIN over 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-19 with iot.history and checks both series with tsfm.data_quality, reporting the usable sample count for each channel. It may characterize the gas trends with tsfm.profile_series. It shortlists candidate pretrained forecasters with tsfm.find_models. It then runs tsfm.run_recipe backtests on co for at least one catalog model and a naive last-value baseline, holding out the final sample, and reports each model's error. The pretrained model is selected only if its error is at least 10% below the baseline's. The agent next runs tsfm.run_recipe with the chosen approach to forecast co and co2 two daily steps ahead with 80% prediction intervals, and computes the projected CO2/CO ratio for each day. The ratio is interpreted as follows: below 3 means likely paper involvement, which calls for an insulation check and a confirmatory resample (the agent may optionally raise this with wo.generate_work_order); 3 to 10 means normal with no action; above 10 means general cellulose ageing for routine review. Fallbacks apply in order. If co2 has fewer than 4 usable samples, the agent forecasts co only, flags any day whose upper bound exceeds the latest co reading by more than 20%, and states that the ratio test couldn't be done. If co has fewer than 4 usable samples, the agent skips the models and reports a linear first-to-last ppm/day extrapolation of co with no interval.

text: Transformer 1 at site MAIN seems to show co rising alongside thermal gases, and I want the right follow-up work on the books without creating duplicates. First, compare co, ethylene and methane at the first and last oil samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, and run a fault classification on the last sample to confirm whether the fault is thermal with paper involved. Then check all open and pending-approval work orders on Transformer 1. If none of them already covers an oil sample retest or an insulation check, create one corrective work order that covers both. Give it priority 2 if the classification comes back T2/T3 with paper involved, and priority 3 otherwise. Code it with the failure code from our catalog that best matches the fault. Assign it to the technician who has the fewest open work orders at MAIN, choosing among the technicians who have worked on Transformer 1 before. Pick a start date within the next 7 days that doesn't land on a day that already has 3 or more scheduled work orders at MAIN. If a matching open work order already exists, don't create a new one. Instead, show me its number, priority and assigned technician, and recommend whether its priority should be raised given the classification. If co is null in either sample, say that paper involvement can't be confirmed and make the work order an oil retest only.
characteristic_form: The agent retrieves co, ethylene and methane with iot.history for Transformer 1 at MAIN over 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-19 and classifies the last sample with fmsr.interpret_dga. It checks for existing coverage using wo.list_workorders filtered by asset and OPEN/APPROVED_PENDING status. If there is no matching work order, it selects a code with wo.get_failure_codes, creates the work order with wo.generate_work_order (priority 2 or 3 per the rule), identifies the prior Transformer 1 technicians from the wo.list_workorders results and compares their workload with wo.get_my_assigned_workorders, checks daily load with wo.get_schedule_calendar to avoid days with 3 or more work orders, and dispatches with wo.assign_technician. If a matching work order exists, it reports that work order and gives a priority recommendation instead. If co is null, the scope drops to an oil retest only.

text: We have a rule for Transformer 1 at MAIN: if it reaches IEEE C57.104 Condition 3, we plan an outage and go to monthly oil sampling. Check whether we're there. Work out TDCG from the latest oil sample using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co only. Use these limits: Condition 1 up to 720 ppm, Condition 2 from 721 to 1920, Condition 3 from 1921 to 4630, and Condition 4 above 4630. If it's Condition 3 or 4, do the following. Look at the MAIN schedule for the 21 days after the latest sample date and propose the 2-day outage window with the fewest scheduled work orders. Create a priority 1 outage and inspection work order for that window, with a note to notify the manufacturer. Create a separate work order for the next monthly DGA sample, dated 30 days after the latest sample. If it's Condition 2, don't plan an outage. Just create a quarterly resample work order. If it's Condition 1, create nothing and tell me how many ppm of headroom we have to 1921. In every case, first check for open work orders on Transformer 1 that already cover an outage or DGA sampling, and don't duplicate them. If one exists, reference it and explain how your recommendation differs. If any of the six gases is null in the latest sample, use its most recent non-null value and flag it as carried forward.
characteristic_form: The agent pulls the six combustible gases with iot.latest_reading, using iot.history to backfill any null gas, and sums TDCG against the stated condition bands. It checks for existing outage or sampling work orders with wo.list_workorders filtered by asset Transformer 1, site MAIN and open status. For Condition 3 or 4, it uses wo.get_schedule_calendar over the 21-day window to pick the least-loaded 2-day window, then calls wo.generate_work_order twice: a priority 1 outage work order with a manufacturer-notification note, and a monthly DGA sample work order. For Condition 2, it creates a single quarterly resample work order. For Condition 1, it creates nothing and reports the headroom to 1921 ppm. Existing work orders are referenced rather than duplicated, and any carried-forward gases are flagged.

text: I'd rather take Transformer 1 at site MAIN out of service once than three times. Pull every open and pending-approval work order on it. For each one, give me the number, description, priority and scheduled date, and say whether it needs the unit de-energized, for example internal inspection, OLTC work or electrical testing, or whether it can be done live, for example oil sampling. Group the outage-needing work orders into bundles. Each bundle must have at least two work orders whose scheduled dates fall within 14 days of each other. For each bundle, propose a single outage date where the MAIN calendar has the fewest other scheduled work orders. Estimate each bundle's total planned hours, using the planned hours on the work orders themselves. Where a work order has no plan, use the average actual hours of closed work orders on Transformer 1. Then check the latest acetylene and hydrogen. If acetylene is above 1 ppm, any bundle with OLTC or inspection work moves to the earliest possible date regardless of calendar load. If fewer than two outage-needing work orders exist, don't bundle anything. Recommend whether each one should be done alone or deferred to the next planned outage, and why.
characteristic_form: The agent lists Transformer 1 work orders with wo.list_workorders (OPEN and APPROVED_PENDING, page_size=0), inspects scope with wo.get_workorder and wo.get_workorder_tasks, and classifies each as outage-required or live-work. It groups outage work into bundles of two or more within 14 days and selects dates with wo.get_schedule_calendar for MAIN. It estimates hours from planned values, using wo.get_workorder_actuals_vs_planned on closed Transformer 1 work orders as the fallback average. It reads acetylene and hydrogen with iot.latest_reading to apply the acetylene > 1 ppm expedite rule. If fewer than two outage work orders exist, it gives standalone or defer recommendations instead of bundles.

text: I suspect our past work orders on Transformer 1 at MAIN have been coded inconsistently, which makes our fault history useless for trending. Pull all work orders on Transformer 1, open and closed, and show me each one's number, description, status and failure code. Then read our failure code catalog and map each code to the closest transformer fault class or failure mode: partial discharge, low-energy arcing, high-energy arcing, oil overheating, core/winding thermal, tap changer wear, moisture ingress, cellulose ageing or oil dielectric degradation. Flag every work order whose code doesn't match its description, and every one that has no code at all, and suggest the correct code for each. Also run a fault classification on the latest oil sample and tell me whether any open work order is coded for a different fault than the gases currently indicate. Only propose recodes, and don't change anything yourself unless the work order is still open and the description clearly names the fault. In that case, update its failure code and list what you changed. If the catalog has no code that fits a fault class, say so and recommend a new code rather than forcing a poor match.
characteristic_form: The agent retrieves all Transformer 1 work orders at MAIN with wo.list_workorders (page_size=0) and wo.get_workorder, and reads the catalog with wo.get_failure_codes. It maps codes to fault classes and failure modes, cross-checked against fmsr.get_failure_modes, and flags mismatched or missing codes. It classifies the latest sample with fmsr.interpret_dga, using data from iot.latest_reading, to compare against open work order coding. It calls wo.update_workorder only for open work orders whose description clearly names the fault. Any catalog gap is reported with a suggested new code.

text: Finance wants a number for Transformer 1 at site MAIN. If the gas trend means we'll need corrective oil work soon, how many hours and how much will it cost? Check whether hydrogen, ethylene and acetylene rose between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, give their daily rates in ppm/day, and project each forward 7 days from the last sample. If any projection crosses its IEEE C57.104 Condition 1 limit, treat corrective work as likely within the week. The limits are 100 ppm for hydrogen, 50 ppm for ethylene and 1 ppm for acetylene. Then look through the closed work order history on Transformer 1 for similar corrective jobs, such as oil treatment, degassing, filtration or internal inspection. Give me their average actual hours, average actual cost and average overrun versus plan, and use those to estimate the likely job. If corrective work is likely and no open work order already covers it, draft a work order carrying that estimate in the notes, and give me the MAIN site's overall backlog and overdue counts so I can see what it competes with. If no similar closed work orders exist, say so. In that case, base the estimate on the average of all closed Transformer 1 work orders and label it low-confidence. If none of the gases is projected to cross a limit, don't create a work order. Just report the estimate as a contingency figure.
characteristic_form: The agent retrieves hydrogen, ethylene and acetylene with iot.history over 2024-01-15 to 2024-01-19, computes the ppm/day rates, and linearly projects each gas 7 days ahead against the 100/50/1 ppm limits. It finds similar closed corrective work orders with wo.list_workorders and wo.get_workorder, and aggregates hours, cost and overrun with wo.get_workorder_costs and wo.get_workorder_actuals_vs_planned. If there are no similar jobs, it averages all closed Transformer 1 work orders and labels the result low-confidence. If a crossing is projected and no open work order covers it, it creates one with wo.generate_work_order carrying the estimate and reports competing load from wo.get_workorder_kpis for MAIN. Otherwise it reports only a contingency estimate.

text:
Several work orders on Transformer 1 at site MAIN are sitting in pending approval, and I want them cleared out properly rather than rubber-stamped. Pull every pending-approval work order on Transformer 1 and give me each one's number, description, priority, reported date and any failure code. Then check the latest oil sample and run a dissolved gas fault classification on it. Use the five fault gases (hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene), and use co to check whether the paper is involved.

Sort each pending work order into one of three outcomes:
- Approve it if its description matches the fault the gases currently indicate, or if it is a routine oil sampling job.
- Cancel it if another open or pending work order on Transformer 1 already covers the same job. Keep the older one, cancel the newer one, and put the older work order's number in the cancellation reason.
- Otherwise, leave it pending and tell me in one sentence why.

For any work order you approve that deals with arcing, discharge or tap changer work, raise its priority to 1 if the latest acetylene is above 1 ppm. Don't change the priority of anything else. Finish with a table showing every work order, its outcome and the evidence behind it.

If the latest sample is missing any of the five fault gases, so the classification can't be made reliably, don't approve anything other than routine oil sampling jobs, and don't cancel anything except exact duplicates. Say which gas was missing. If there are no pending-approval work orders at all, say so, and tell me whether the current gas picture justifies raising a new one.
characteristic_form: The agent calls wo.list_workorders (site_id=MAIN, asset_num=Transformer 1, status=APPROVED_PENDING, page_size=0) and wo.get_workorder for details. It also calls wo.list_workorders with status=OPEN to find duplicates. It retrieves the latest DGA values with iot.latest_reading and classifies the fault with fmsr.interpret_dga, using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene for the IEC 60599 class and co for paper involvement. Each pending work order has one of three outcomes: approved with wo.approve_workorder, cancelled as a newer duplicate with wo.cancel_workorder and the older WO number in the reason, or left pending with a justification. For approved arcing, discharge or OLTC work orders, priority is set to 1 with wo.update_workorder only if acetylene exceeds 1 ppm. Fallback when any of the five fault gases is null: only routine sampling WOs are approved, only exact duplicates are cancelled, and the missing gas is named. Fallback when no pending WOs exist: the agent says so and advises whether the DGA condition justifies a new WO. The output is a per-WO outcome table with its supporting evidence.

text:
I'm worried that urgent work on Transformer 1 at site MAIN is stuck behind an overloaded technician. Give me the MAIN site's work order KPIs for the last 6 months, including backlog, overdue count and average completion time. Then list every open work order on Transformer 1 with its number, description, priority, scheduled date and assigned technician, and flag which ones are overdue.

For each technician assigned to those work orders, count how many open work orders they currently hold at MAIN. Anyone holding more than 5 counts as overloaded.

Next, work out TDCG from the latest oil sample using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co only. Use these limits: Condition 1 up to 720 ppm, Condition 2 from 721 to 1920, Condition 3 from 1921 to 4630, and Condition 4 above 4630.

If Transformer 1 is at Condition 2 or higher, do the following for any overdue work order on it that sits with an overloaded technician. Reassign it to the technician with the fewest open work orders at MAIN, choosing among those who have worked on Transformer 1 before and are not overloaded. Give it a start date within the next 7 days that avoids any day with 3 or more scheduled work orders at MAIN. If it is Condition 1, don't reassign anything. Just list the overdue items and recommend a catch-up order, ranked by priority and then by how late they are.

If every technician with Transformer 1 history is overloaded, don't reassign. Tell me who is least loaded and recommend bringing in outside help. If any of the six gases is null in the latest sample, use its most recent non-null value and flag it as carried forward.
characteristic_form: The agent calls wo.get_workorder_kpis (site_id=MAIN, period_months=6) for backlog, overdue and completion metrics. It calls wo.list_workorders (asset_num=Transformer 1, status=OPEN) and wo.get_workorder to get assignees and scheduled dates, then flags overdue items. It counts each technician's open load with wo.get_my_assigned_workorders (open_only=true, site_id=MAIN) and marks anyone with more than 5 as overloaded. It identifies technicians with Transformer 1 history from closed WOs via wo.list_workorders. It computes TDCG from iot.latest_reading using the six combustible gases, carrying forward nulls from iot.history with a flag, and maps the total to the IEEE C57.104 condition. At Condition 2 or higher, overdue WOs held by overloaded technicians are reassigned with wo.assign_technician to the least-loaded, non-overloaded technician with Transformer 1 history. The new start date is within 7 days, chosen from wo.get_schedule_calendar to avoid days with 3 or more scheduled WOs. At Condition 1, the agent only lists overdue items and gives a catch-up ranking by priority and then lateness. Fallback: if every qualified technician is overloaded, no reassignment is made, and the agent names the least-loaded technician and recommends outside help.

text:
I think the oil in Transformer 1 at site MAIN may be losing its insulating strength, and I need to decide whether to plan an oil reconditioning before it becomes a real problem.

First, check dielectric_rigidity and interfacial_v between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000 for gaps. Tell me how many usable samples each has. Then forecast both 3 days ahead, one step per day, with an 80% prediction interval for each day, and tell me whether each one is heading down.

Separately, work out a health index and condition category from the latest oil sample. Also tell me whether hydrogen or acetylene in that sample suggests discharge activity in the weakened oil.

Only recommend reconditioning if both signals point to risk: at least one of the two forecasts is falling, and the health index is fair or worse. If that happens:
- Check the work order history on Transformer 1 for any oil filtration, degassing or regeneration in the past 12 months.
- If there was none, create one work order covering oil reconditioning plus a confirmatory oil quality test.
- Assign it to a technician who has worked on Transformer 1 before.
- If there was one, don't create a new work order. Give me its number and date, and say the oil may be degrading faster than expected.

If only one of the two signals points to risk, don't create anything. Recommend an oil quality retest instead and tell me which signal disagreed.

If either channel has fewer than 4 usable samples, don't run a model on it. Report its first-to-last change per day as a linear extrapolation with no interval, and say so.
characteristic_form: The agent should confirm the window with iot.stream_extent for Transformer 1 at MAIN and pull dielectric_rigidity and interfacial_v with iot.history over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. It should check completeness, either with tsfm.data_quality on the materialized series or by counting non-null values. For any channel with at least 4 usable samples, it should pick a forecaster with tsfm.find_models and run a 3-step forecast with 80% intervals using tsfm.run_recipe. For channels with fewer than 4 samples, it should report a linear first-to-last rate labelled as extrapolation. It should get the latest sample with iot.latest_reading and call fmsr.predict_health_index with hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, methane, co, co2, ethylene, ethane, acetylene, dbds, interfacial_v and dielectric_rigidity from that sample, and should not invent missing inputs. It should comment on hydrogen and acetylene as discharge indicators. The decision requires both a falling forecast and a health category of fair or worse. Only then should it call wo.list_workorders on Transformer 1 to look for oil treatment in the past 12 months. If there was none, it should call wo.generate_work_order for reconditioning plus a confirmatory test, then wo.assign_technician using a labor code taken from prior Transformer 1 work orders. If there was a recent treatment, it should create nothing and report that work order's number and date. If only one signal indicates risk, it should create no work order, recommend a retest and name the disagreeing signal.

text:
The last maintenance job on Transformer 1 at site MAIN was supposed to deal with the gassing, and I want to know whether it actually worked.

Find the most recently closed work order on Transformer 1. Give me its number, description, completion date, resolution notes and failure code, and tell me which fault it was meant to fix.

Then look at the oil samples taken after that date, within 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. Use hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co. Screen hydrogen, acetylene and co for anomalous samples with a proper anomaly detection model rather than a fixed threshold. Separately, run a dissolved gas fault classification on the latest complete sample and compare its fault class with the fault the job was meant to fix.

Decide as follows:
- If both checks point to trouble, meaning at least one anomaly is flagged and the classification still shows the same fault or a higher-energy one, call the fix ineffective. Create a priority 2 corrective follow-up work order that references the original work order number, and code it with the closest failure code from our catalog.
- If only one of the two checks points to trouble, don't create a corrective job. Recommend a confirmatory oil resample within 7 days and say which check disagreed.
- If neither points to trouble, say the fix appears to have held.

If the closed job was oil filtration, degassing or regeneration, the gas levels will have been reset. In that case, judge the result on the rate of change after the job, not on absolute levels, and say you did so.

If no work order on Transformer 1 was closed before or during the window, say so, use all samples in the window, and give only the classification and anomaly result without a verdict on any fix. If fewer than 4 samples fall after the completion date, skip the anomaly model and compare the first and last post-job values instead.
characteristic_form: The agent should call wo.list_workorders filtered to asset Transformer 1 at MAIN, identify the most recently closed work order, and read its completion date, resolution notes and failure code from the returned work order details. It should confirm the post-job sample range with iot.stream_extent and pull hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co with iot.history, restricted to samples after the completion date and within 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. If at least 4 samples remain, it should select a detector with tsfm.find_models(task_id='tsfm_anomaly_detection') and screen hydrogen, acetylene and co with tsfm.run_recipe. Otherwise it should compare first and last values. It should call fmsr.interpret_dga on the latest complete sample and compare the IEC class with the fault the original job targeted. The job counts as ineffective only when both the anomaly check and the classification indicate trouble. In that case it should look up a code with wo.get_failure_codes and create a priority 2 follow-up with wo.generate_work_order that references the original work order. If the two checks disagree, it should recommend a resample within 7 days and create no corrective order. For filtration or degassing jobs, it should judge on post-job rates rather than absolute levels. If no closed work order exists, it should report classification and anomaly results only, with no verdict on a fix.

text:
I want to set the next oil sampling date for Transformer 1 at site MAIN based on how fast the gases are actually growing, not on a fixed calendar.

Using the samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, work out TDCG for every sample. Use only hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene, acetylene and co, and leave out co2, oxygen and nitrogen. Give me the TDCG rate in ppm/day between the first and last sample, and name the gas that contributes most to the increase.

Before trusting that rate, screen the six gases for anomalous samples. If a single anomalous sample is driving the rise, recompute the rate without it and show me both numbers.

Set the interval with this rule:
- Under 10 ppm/day: next sample in 90 days.
- 10 to 30 ppm/day: next sample in 30 days.
- Above 30 ppm/day: next sample in 7 days.

If the rate with and without the anomalous sample lands in different bands, don't escalate on the higher one. Use the lower band's interval and add a confirmatory resample within 7 days to settle it.

Also run a fault classification on the latest complete sample. If it comes back D1, D2 or T3, use 7 days no matter what the rate says.

Then check open work orders on Transformer 1. If a sampling job is already open, don't create another. Tell me its number and date, and whether it should move earlier. Otherwise, pick the first day on or after the target date where MAIN has fewer than 3 scheduled work orders, create the sampling work order for that day, and assign a technician who has sampled Transformer 1 before.

If fewer than two samples in the window have all six gases, say the rate can't be computed. In that case, base the interval on the classification alone: 7 days for D1, D2 or T3, and 30 days otherwise.
characteristic_form: The agent should confirm the window with iot.stream_extent for Transformer 1 at MAIN and pull the six combustible gases with iot.history over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. It should compute per-sample TDCG, excluding co2, oxygen and nitrogen, calculate the first-to-last rate in ppm/day, and name the largest contributing gas. It should screen the gases for anomalies using tsfm.find_models(task_id='tsfm_anomaly_detection') and tsfm.run_recipe, and recompute the rate without any single dominant anomalous sample. It should call fmsr.interpret_dga on the latest complete sample. The rate band sets the interval (90, 30 or 7 days). If the two rates fall in different bands, the lower band's interval applies plus a confirmatory resample. A D1, D2 or T3 class overrides the interval to 7 days. It should check wo.list_workorders for an existing open sampling job and avoid duplicating it. It should use wo.get_schedule_calendar at MAIN to find the first day on or after the target date with fewer than 3 scheduled work orders, then call wo.generate_work_order and wo.assign_technician with a labor code from prior Transformer 1 sampling work. If fewer than two complete samples exist, it should report that the rate is not computable and base the interval on the classification alone.

text:
We're short on crews this month, and I'd like to push the next planned job on Transformer 1 at site MAIN back by 30 days. Tell me whether that's safe.

Find the open or pending-approval work order on Transformer 1 with the earliest scheduled date. Give me its number, description, priority and scheduled date. If it's an oil sampling or DGA job, don't defer it under any circumstances. Just say why.

Otherwise, build two separate pieces of evidence:
1. Using the samples between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, forecast hydrogen, ethylene and acetylene 7 days ahead from the last sample, with an 80% upper bound. Compare the upper bounds with the IEEE C57.104 Condition 1 limits of 100 ppm for hydrogen, 50 ppm for ethylene and 1 ppm for acetylene.
2. Run a dissolved gas fault classification on the latest complete sample, using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene.

Decide as follows:
- Approve the deferral only if no upper bound crosses its limit and the class is not D1, D2 or T3. In that case, find a day about 30 days after the current scheduled date where MAIN has fewer than 3 scheduled work orders. Add a note to the work order with the proposed new date and the evidence behind it.
- If both pieces of evidence point to risk, keep the original date. Raise the priority to 1 if acetylene is the gas crossing its limit.
- If they disagree, keep the original date, don't change the priority, and recommend a confirmatory oil resample before revisiting the deferral.

If any of the three gases has fewer than 4 usable samples, don't model it. Project its last value forward 7 days using the average daily change between the first and last samples, and label it as a linear extrapolation with no interval.
characteristic_form: The agent should call wo.list_workorders for Transformer 1 at MAIN with status OPEN and APPROVED_PENDING, and select the work order with the earliest scheduled date. If that work order is a sampling or DGA job, the agent should refuse the deferral. Otherwise it should pull hydrogen, ethylene and acetylene with iot.history over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, check sample counts, and for series with at least 4 usable samples select a model with tsfm.find_models and run a 7-day forecast with 80% intervals via tsfm.run_recipe. Series with fewer samples get a labelled linear extrapolation. It should compare the upper bounds with the 100, 50 and 1 ppm limits. It should call fmsr.interpret_dga on the latest complete sample, taken from iot.latest_reading or iot.history. Deferral is allowed only when both signals are benign. In that case it should use wo.get_schedule_calendar to find a date about 30 days later with fewer than 3 scheduled work orders and record it with wo.update_workorder notes. If both signals indicate risk, it should keep the date and raise the priority to 1 via wo.update_workorder if acetylene crosses its limit. If the signals disagree, it should keep the date and priority unchanged and recommend a resample.

text:
Oxygen and nitrogen in Transformer 1's oil at site MAIN might be creeping up, which could mean a leaking gasket or a breather or conservator problem letting air in. I'd like to know before the oil oxidizes.

Between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, give me the first and last values of oxygen and nitrogen, and the daily change for each. Then look at how they move together with top-oil temperature (oti) and ambient (ati). I want to know whether the rise simply follows temperature swings, as normal thermal breathing would, or happens independently of them.

Separately, check whether the oil is already suffering from oxidation:
- Look at the trend in interfacial_v.
- Work out the CO2/CO ratio at the last sample.
- Get a health index and condition category from the latest sample.

Treat a seal leak as likely only if oxygen and nitrogen both rose and the rise is not explained by temperature. If so, first check open work orders on Transformer 1 for any existing gasket, breather or conservator inspection. If one exists, give me its number and don't duplicate it. Otherwise, create an inspection work order covering gaskets, the conservator and the breather. Make it priority 2 if interfacial_v fell over the window or the health index is fair or worse, and priority 3 otherwise.

If only one of the two gases rose, or the rise tracks temperature, don't create a work order. Recommend a resample taken with a gas-tight syringe to rule out sampling contamination, and say which condition wasn't met.

If oxygen has no data in the window, say that air ingress can't be properly assessed. Give a nitrogen-only view labelled low confidence, and don't create a work order.
characteristic_form: The agent should confirm the window with iot.stream_extent for Transformer 1 at MAIN and retrieve oxygen, nitrogen, oti, ati, interfacial_v, co and co2 with iot.history over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. It may use iot.sensor_stats for summaries. It should report first and last values and daily changes for oxygen and nitrogen. It should materialize the series and run tsfm.profile_series on the dissolved-air group (oxygen, nitrogen) alongside the temperature group (oti, ati) to judge whether the gas rise tracks temperature. It should compute the CO2/CO ratio at the last sample and the interfacial_v trend, and call fmsr.predict_health_index with the latest sample values from iot.latest_reading. A seal leak is concluded only when both gases rose and the rise is independent of temperature. The agent should then check wo.list_workorders for existing seal, breather or conservator inspections before calling wo.generate_work_order. The work order is priority 2 if interfacial_v fell or the health index is fair or worse, and priority 3 otherwise. If the conditions are not met, the agent should create no work order and recommend a gas-tight resample. If oxygen has no data, it should give a low-confidence nitrogen-only assessment and create no work order.

text:
I'm starting to suspect the cooling on Transformer 1 at site MAIN, such as fans, radiators or oil pumps, rather than anything inside the tank. Check this for me before I send a crew out.

Between 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 and 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000, work out the top-oil rise over ambient (oti minus ati) for every sample. For each sample, give it alongside the total phase current (il1 + il2 + il3). Then tell me whether the rise is climbing while the current stays roughly flat, meaning total current changes by less than 10% from first to last sample. That pattern points to lost cooling capacity rather than load.

Forecast the oti-minus-ati rise 2 days ahead, one step per day, with an 80% upper bound. Then check whether oti itself would get closer to its alarm reading (oti_a) than it is today.

Separately, run a dissolved gas fault classification on the latest complete sample using hydrogen, methane, ethane, ethylene and acetylene. This tells me whether there's an internal thermal fault instead.

Decide as follows:
- Cooling problem: the rise is climbing with flat current, and the gas class is not T2, T3, D1 or D2. First check open work orders on Transformer 1 for an existing cooling system inspection. If there's none, create one at priority 3, or priority 2 if the forecast upper bound brings oti within 5 °C of oti_a.
- Internal fault: the gas class is T2, T3, D1 or D2. Don't raise a cooling work order. Tell me the rise pattern is more likely a symptom of an internal fault and recommend a confirmatory oil resample.
- Rise doesn't climb: say that cooling looks healthy and create nothing.

If oti or ati has fewer than 4 non-null samples, don't forecast. Report the first-to-last change in the rise per day as a linear extrapolation with no interval.
characteristic_form: Coordinated iot, tsfm, fmsr and wo workflow. The agent confirms the window with iot.stream_extent and retrieves oti, ati, oti_a, il1, il2 and il3 per sample with iot.history over 2024-01-15T00:00:00.000000 to 2024-01-19T00:00:00.000000. It computes the oti minus ati rise and the total phase current for each sample, and tests whether current changed by less than 10% while the rise increased.
